paper_title: Sub-monolayer tracking of molecular states at buried interfaces

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Phenomena responsible for emerging technologies originate from novel molecular states at buried interfaces. Yet quantitatively resolving these features is out of reach in most cases. Resonant scattering has demonstrated sensitivity to these local states but is limited due to a lack of accurate interpretive models. We leverage a machine learning (ML)-optimized optical model to analyze polarized resonant soft X-ray scattering (RSoXS) from molecular thin films. This new analysis establishes the direct and quantitative interpretation of molecular orientation, chemical identity and packing states as a function of depth with sub-monolayer resolution - reaching beyond the diffraction limit via locking energy and polarization through the optical model. From our analysis, we discover a gradient evolution of molecular orientation and packing emerging from the interface, indicative of competing surface versus bulk growth dynamics and contradicting hypotheses of substrate patterning. This nondestructive insight into buried interfacial formation and final state opens possibilities in controlling interfacial states and phenomena in next-generation technologies.

For example, in extreme-ultraviolet photoresists the chemical gradient at the edge of the latent image limits for microprocessors.6,7 In organic devices such as solar cells, LEDs, transistors, and spin valves the orientation and conformation of the molecular monolayer at the interface governs emergent electronic states that control charge generation, recombination, transport, and spin hybridization respectively.1,2,810 In bioand chemical sensing, molecular states at buried interfaces have resulted in novel ionic transport dynamics.1113 Controlling molecular states directly at these interfaces is, therefore, central to advancing each of these technologies. achievable process size the few techniques Unfortunately, that resolve buried interfacial structure, such as atom probe tomography are laborious, highly destructive, and cant resolve details of bonding states and their orientations.14 Lacking direct probe, novel interfacial molecular states (e.g. orientation and packing) are thought to be achieved via substrate patterning effects,1517 similar to atomic epitaxial growth. Studies have attempted to access the buried molecular state by measuring deposition at coverage checkpoints 1820 with in situ measurements resolving density the patterning hypothesis.18 Yet other work suggests these coverage snapshots only describe the exposed molecular layers in transient state that change once buried, 19,20 leaving the mechanisms governing formation and control of interfacial states unresolved. that contradict stratification RSoXS, tuned to the energies of electronic transitions into unoccupied molecular orbitals can non-destructively reveal the chemical, electronic, and physical states within these buried structures7,21,22. Therefore, analyses retreat to single diagnostic resonance which cannot distinguish chemical species nor orientation unless simplifying assumptions are made. 23,28,29 Worse, buried interfacial layer is typically required to accurately fit the data which is assumed to be comprised of contaminants or oxidation,23,24,26,27 and there is no way to determine if these layers are real or merely limitation of the soft X-rays diffraction limit which sets the smallest resolvable feature by the scatterers wavelength, in this case, several nanometers. Recently, near edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) spectroscopy measurements have been used to construct an Edisonian optical model, enabling the orientation state to be inferred though secondary analysis of the optical parameters, although the above limitations remain.2325,27,30 Alternative approaches arrive at the optical model from density functional theory (DFT), yet are limited by fundamental computational inaccuracies.3133 Recently, we have demonstrated that MLrefined DFT optical models can quantitatively reproduce angleresolved (AR) NEXAFS measurements of polycrystalline thin films with different orientation and crystal phases while retaining individual bond identity and orientation.34 Here we construct and apply an ML-DFT optical model in RSoXS analysis to directly quantify molecular chemical identity, orientation and density as function of depth in molecular thin film. From these results, we conclude that the DFT model achieves drastic statistical improvement in fit quality with 17x fewer parameters and 10x smaller parameter uncertainties, while presenting directly interpretable results that are useful to interrogate the molecular state. Sub-monolayer interfacial physics Without needing to account for unique chemical species at the boundaries of the ZnPc bulk layer, the independent slab model is no longer physically motivated. Instead, we develop single slab gradient model based on the physics of continuous second order transition from pinned molecular state due to surface energies that evolve toward an energy-minimized state in the bulk (derivation in SI Sec. 6). This results in description physically matched to an evolving growth front during deposition with each deposited layer taking its orientation from those beneath it. This gradient model resolves orientation as smooth function of depth, parameterized by the bulk state and two exponentials that transition over characteristic lengths 𝜏 toward the pinned state at each interface. Besides incorporating the physics at play during deposition, this structural model also has fewer parameters than the slab model. The fit using the graded interface model (with ML-DFT modeling optics) is compared to the slab model in Fig. 4a for the diagnostic profile at 283.7 eV, together with the resonant series but neglecting the rest of the data. Notably, the erroneous phase shift of the fringes in the slab model is removed in the gradient model and the Brewster angle is reproduced significantly better than the slab model. These fit improvements along with the reduced number of parameters enable the best goodness of fit, indicating this model recovers the true orientation and density gradient within the sample more accurately than what the traditional slab picture can achieve. Notably, the entire film is only 15 monolayers thick with the substrate surface energy affecting region equivalent to single monolayer. However, the fact that the graded interface model fits better than the discrete slab model reveals that the continuous density and orientation variation over that region represents real structural variation resolved by this analysis. In fact, the unique tilt in the last few angstroms at the interface, can only manifest with sub-monolayer coverage of ZnPc molecules that are pinned relatively flat on the substrate. This confined feature is well below the experimental diffraction limit (2𝜋 𝑞𝑚𝑎𝑥 > 23Å). However, scattering from such features still modify the amplitude and phase of the measured fringes. Fisher sensitivity analysis (Fig. S13) determines that these submonolayer features are uniquely captured and constrained by our ML-DFT optical model which locks these effects as function of energy and polarization to enable recovery of the molecular state below the diffraction limit. Surface vs bulk dynamics in film growth These results are direct evidence against the model of substrate patterning of bulk molecular orientation and provide evidence toward an alternative model that incorporates intermolecular interactions at the growth front. One explanation for our results is that the orientation planar molecule adopts during deposition reflects competition between the substrate adhesion, which favors face-on alignment and intermolecular 𝜋 𝜋 cohesion, which favors edge-on packing. The gradient then traces the crossover from low dimensional interfacial coupling to the three-dimensional growth mechanism that sets the bulk texture. The lower density and face-on alignment at the interface indicates that the packing state here is not the relaxed herringbone but possibly primordial face-on brickstone packing structure which typically exhibits such properties.18 We expect that evaluating these effects on interfacial states in molecular systems will enable control of emergent phenomena at these interfaces, for example, charge generation and recombination in organic solar cells and OLED technologies1,2 or charge and ion transport in transistors8 or electrochemical devices.1113,54,55 The same sub-monolayer sensitivity extends directly to self-assembled monolayers, where incomplete or defective coverage during assembly is now recognized as the limiting factor for both efficiency and thermal stability in stateof-the-art perovskite solar cell devices.9 More broadly the analysis can be applied to any interface, polymer, alloy, or fewlayer system whose function depends on coverage-dependent structure that bulk-averaged measurement cannot resolve. The surface densification measured here, along with an orientation approaching the magic angle also indicates distinct state from the bulk, where the higher density and disorder may be caused by the physics of surface tension during deposition. In this case, these boundary layers are not the adventitious hydrocarbon contamination nor oxidation to which filmaveraged analyses and other RSoXS studies customarily assign them27,56 but rather potentially disordered state before the ZnPc molecules fully crystalize. Moreover, this demonstrates that in studies characterizing structure of films deposited with varying coverages1820 do not measure in continuously deposited film, since both substrate and free surface energetics pull the state away from the final buried states. the state expected The new RSoXS analysis provides depth sensitivity to buried molecular state applied in broad range of physical conditions, allowing quantitative studies of interfacial phenomena like crystal growth, kinetic deposition, and solvent interaction. The same construction extends to molecules with additional orientational and chemical freedom, to polymers, alloys, and mixed oxidation states or orbital hybridization affecting 5 unoccupied molecular orbitals. The analysis is, furthermore, applicable to scattering geometries beyond reflectivity, enabling local chemical, electronic, and physical analyses of inaccessible buried interfaces that govern function across material systems and nanostructures. Connecting scattering features that vary with energy and polarization, our ML-DFT optical model can not only provide these states directly but also push the resolution well beyond the traditional diffraction limit. interprets In summary, we introduce resonant X-ray scattering analysis that directly the quantitative physiochemical molecular state in buried nanostructure based on an MLrefined DFT optical model. The analysis dramatically increases the precision and resolution beyond the diffraction limit, so that molecular state at an interface can be directly characterized. Applying this analysis to ZnPc films, we find that hypotheses of chemical contamination at the film surface and buried interface are rejected in favor of the molecules exhibiting novel packing and orientational state. Introducing structural model based on the dynamics of film growth, we reveal evidence to reject hypotheses of substrate patterning of the bulk packing state replaced with competition between 2D versus 3D film growth dynamics that determines the interfacial evolution of the molecular states. This statistical analysis of the final buried molecular state contrasts with checkpoint studies that track growth front that is likely only in temporary state. We envision this new non-destructive view inside buried interfaces and structures will lead to exquisite control of novel functionalities. sections.content: Film growth: Small molecule ZnPc (C32H16N8Zn sourced from Sigma Aldrich) with purity 99.5% was further purified in the physical vapor deposition (PVD) chamber (base pressure < 1 107 Torr) by gradually heating, approaching ZnPc sublimation temperature over approximately an hour until no further off gassing of contaminants were detected by the quartz crystal monitor (QCM). Thin films (20 nm measured by QCM) of ZnPc were deposited at . 2 Å/𝑠 on high conductivity polished Si wafers (University Wafers). Wafers were cleaved 1 cm 3 cm and cleaned via sonication in deionized water, acetone and isopropyl alcohols before 30 min UV ozone bake. ZnPc was either deposited directly onto these wafers to create the herringbone crystal structure, or onto thin Copper Iodide (CuI, 3nm) patterning layer producing face on brick-stone polymorph. Substrate temperature was either set to the ambient room temperature (24 C), by liquid nitrogen cooling (-50 C), or by thermal substrate heating (100 C). For brick-stone samples, CuI and ZnPc depositions were performed sequentially under the same vacuum, with 20 min between depositions to return to the base pressure. Films for RSoXS were stored under an inert N2 atmosphere and transported to the ALS under vacuum. Auxiliary pre characterization measurements were performed on separate films from the same batch to avoid surface contamination and oxidation prior to RSoXS. VASE: Variable angle spectroscopic ellipsometry (VASE) (Fig S1) was performed using J.A. Woollam alpha-SE to pre characterize layer thickness and molecular orientation. Data was collected at three incidences (65, 70, & 75) targeting sample from the same PVD batch and measured using vendor supplied CompleteEase software. Optical constants where modeled using B-spline producing similar spectra to literature.57 The results and analysis of VASE data are discussed in SI Sec. 1.1. GIXRD: Grazing incidence wide angle x-ray diffraction (GIXRD) measurements (Fig S2) were performed at Washington State University on Xenocs Xeuss 3.0 with focused Cu X-ray source (𝜆 = 1.5418 Å), under vacuum at 72 mm sampledetector distance with incident angle set to 0.2. The sample-todetector distance and beam center were calibrated with silverbehenate standard. 1D reduction of GIWAXS images was done using NIKA software 58 and peak positions were obtained by fitting Gaussian line shapes to the reduced profiles. The lamellar reflection lies along the 𝑞𝑧 and the 𝜋 𝜋 reflection is in plane corresponding with the edge on texture of the 𝛼 herringbone polymorph reported for vacuum deposited ZnPc and CuPc.59 The results and analysis of GIXRD data are discussed in SI Sec. 1.2. AFM: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) height maps were acquired on Bruker Dimension Icon in tapping mode with TESPA-V2 SAMPLE probe. Scans where processed using Gwyddion60 to extract root-mean-square (RMS) roughness values. Film morphologies and RMS roughness values were used to pre-characterize film surface roughness and morphology RSoXS measurements. The surface topology is included in Fig S4 and the discussion in SI Sec. 1.3 and 1.4. wafers.61 Samples where grown under the same conditions Spectra were collected at five sample alignments with respect to the incident electric field polarization vector with respect to the (20, 40, 55, 70, & 90). NEXAFS was surface normal collected over the energy range of 270-350 eV and normalized to the energy dependent intensity fluctuation and optical loss via direct photodiode measurement, and Au mesh drain current. Mass absorption was computed via normalization in the pre and post edge regions to the bare atom mass absorption of ZnPc as extracted from the CXRO Henke atomic scattering factors.62 Molecular tilt angle was extracted via the DFT cluster and refinement process. As the final step of the refinement process, the molecular polar tilt angle 𝛾 is fit using the TDM cluster orientations prescribed by DFT providing measure of the molecular orientation (Fig S5). This fit produces reduces 𝜒2 goodness of fit statistic of .213 indicating very good agreement between the model and experimental data. The molecular tilt angle of 74 agrees with all other characterizations of the ZnPc face on herringbone polymorph described in this study and is taken as the coarse-grained molecular orientation within the films measured under RSoXS (full analysis in SI Sec. 3). Density Functional Theory: time independent transition potential calculation using the StoBe library was performed on single molecule of ZnPc. HCH approach sets the manifold of transition energies, along with each TDM and oscillator strength, while the Δ𝐾𝑆 method is used to fix the absolute energy associated with each transition. For details see our previous work.34 The molecular geometry was extracted from crystallographic structure file (.cif)63 as it produced results with higher to thermodynamically relaxed structures, or those relaxed from molecular force fields. The final calculation results are provided in SI Sec. 1.6. to experiment compared initial agreement is constructed ML-clustering and refinement: The ML optimized optical tensor though hierarchical agglomerative clustering to extract principle TDM clusters. Exact implementation details may be found on GitHub or through our previous work.34,64 TDM clusters are sequentially refined to quantitative agreement with experimental AR-NEXAFS by fitting oscillator strength, excitation energy, and TDM orientation. Optimal hyperparameters, oscillator strength investigated by threshold and overlap percentage were evaluating this best fit metric on an even grid 𝑂𝑆 [0, 10] & 𝑂𝑉𝑃 [25,75] with details in SI Sec 3.1 and highlighted in Fig S7. From the family of hyperparameters that perform well on this metric, the refinement performance is additionally weighted by the adherence to the original DFT spectra and TDM cluster families such that the refinement step does not significantly alter the DFT calculation. Here we chose the best clustering parameters of 𝑂𝑆 = 0.25 and 𝑂𝑉𝑃 = 52.5 with the full evaluation matrix in Fig. S7. In general, we find good clustering and convergence for all 𝑂𝑉𝑃 [55,50], with significantly worse performance outside of these bounds. Moreover, we find that 𝑂𝑆 [. 1,8] performed similarly, yet parameter agreement with originating DFT degrades rapid for larger 𝑂𝑆, while the refinement never converse for 𝑂𝑆 < .1. NEXAFS spectroscopy: NEXAFS spectra were collected at the Soft X-ray Spectroscopy (SXR) beamline of the Australian Synchrotron, part of ANSTO in total electron yield mode on Si RSoXS collection: Polarized resonant soft x-ray reflectivity was measured at beamline 11.0.1.2 of the Advanced Light Source, the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, following 8 procedure established by Ferron et al.27 Samples are transferred from inert storage to the end station where specular reflectance is captured on the CCD area detector with thermals managed by thermos-electric cooling. The sample surface is aligned to the goniometer axis of rotation by an iterative process that refines the sample rotation and height. Incident flux was attenuated using the scatter slits together with the higher order suppressor to avoid detector damage. Because the total reflectance varies by more than the detectors dynamic range, reflectivity is captured in overlapping 𝒒 subsets with suppressor settings and exposure time raised at each boundary once reflectivity reaches the noise floor. Data is collected first in polarization and then in polarization beginning at 250 eV below the carbon edge and stepping upward though the resonance, for 21 photon energies collected in batches of five energies with the axis of rotation alignment was reevaluated between energy batches. Upon polarization change, optics were allowed to re equilibrate to the new heat load for 30 min before alignment was recalibrated. The complete dataset was acquired within single 12 shift. Photon energy transmission NEXAFS of was calibrated against polystyrene standard at the beginning and at the end of the shift with no discernable shift, bounding the energy drift over the experiment to the width of the primary polystyrene feature. the RSoXS reduction: Reflectance was reduced from the twodimensional detector the RSoXS-reduce images using package.65 The specular spot was located on each frame and its intensity integrated over fixed region of interest. An equal region displaced along the same detector row provided the background, so that subtraction removes the systematic rowwise readout offset in addition to dark current and stray light. Reflectance was then formed by dividing the backgroundcorrected specular intensity by the incident 𝐼0 recorded at the start of each reflectivity profile through the averaging of five direct beam measurements. At each energy, full multi-decade reflectivity profiles are constructed by properly scaling and joining the overlapping 𝒒subsets measured at different attenuation and exposure time. An effective 𝐼0 is computed from the four overlapping points, and the subsets were joined to form singular continuous reflectivity profile for each measured energy. Reported uncertainties combine per-pixel effective 𝐼0 with 𝒒-dependent envelope accounting for the increasing ambiguity between specular and diffuse reflectivity at higher 𝒒 using the following equation: 𝜎(𝐸, 𝒒) = 𝑎𝑅𝑒𝑥𝑝(𝐸, 𝒒) + 𝑏𝒒 (5) With 𝑎 = .08 and 𝑏 = .5 106, which is feasible approximation for experimental error under these considerations (discussion in SI Sec. 5.3). RSoXS structural and optical modeling: Reflectivity is computed from the 4x4 transfer matrix using the refloxide package.66 The film was modeled as three ZnPc slabs, denoted surface, bulk and interface, on native SiO2 layer and semiinfinite Si substrate. Thickness and roughness of each ZnPc slab together with the oxide thickness and roughness give eight structural parameters. Reflection and transmission coefficients were computed at each photon energy and scattering vector with the 4x4 transfer matrix formalism matching boundary conditions at the five interfaces, with interfacial toughness entering in the Nevot-Croce sense as an exponential attenuation representing off-specular diffuse scattering from faceted interface.67 Vacuum, silicon, silicon dioxide, and silicon where assigned to tabulated bare atom optical constants,62 with an energyindependent density allowed to vary within (2, 2.8) cm-3 to accommodate stochiometric deviation from the tabulated values. The forward model was evaluated using refloxide, and the objective and parameter machinery where provided by refnx.68 Two optical parameterizations were compared on this identical structure. The free tensor parameterization assigns each ZnPc slab an independent birefringence, dichroism, isotropic 𝛽 and isotropic 𝛿 at every measured energy, constraining to ranges dictated by the starting optical model, amounting to 252 optical tensor components. The DFT parameterization instead describes each slab energy-independently by molecular orientation and density, with one energy offset term common to all layers absorbing the calibrated difference between the NEXAFS and RSoXS instruments, amounting to seven parameters for all three slabs. detailed parameter accounting and comparison with prior art is discussed in SI Sec. 5.4. Experimental corrections were applied per energy and per polarization as normalization scale factor and an angle-ofincidence offset, following Ferron et al.,27 adding four terms per energy at 84 in total. The refinement therefore varies 101 parameters for the DFT model and 350 for the free tensor model. Bound on the correction terms, and the correlations they induce are described in SI Sec. 5.4. All energies and polarizations are co-refined against single global objective, so that the structural parameters are shared across the dataset and only the optical and correction terms carry energy indices. The log-likelihood assumed Gaussian errors at the uncertainties propagated though reduction, and all varying parameters were assigned uniform priors over their stated bounds. The maximum likelihood parameter set was located by differential evolution over the full bounded space, in parallel with deferred population updating and local polish step using the L-BFGS-B algorithm, avoiding dependency on initial conditions. Reported parameter uncertainties are then taken from the inversion of the Hessian evaluated in the final polish step. Model comparison uses reduced chi square together with the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. Unit cell construction: Unit cells used for molecular dynamics simulations are constructed though fusion of GIXRD 𝑑-spacings with literature unit cells. The rigid ZnPc molecule originates from the same 𝛽-ZnPc (Fig S13a) crystallographic results used for DFT simulations.63 Lennard-Jones parameters are GAFF2, with UFF for the Zn coordination center. Charges are fitted using the B3LYP/def2-SVP electrostatic potentials and used to set the electrostatic repulsion between molecules. The 𝛽-ZnPc stable polymorph with known structure serves only as the validation target. suitable unit cell was constructed from the chemically similar 𝛼-CuPc by placing rigid ZnPc molecules within the CuPc unit cell. Lattice parameters and are set by the lamellar spacing (002), with set by the 𝜋 𝜋 packing. The molecular tilt angle is scanned and compared to the GIXRD patterns though fiber-texture forward model, with other unit cell angles set by minimizing the lattice energy (UFF+ESP). The resulting lattice parameters are tabulated in 9 Table SIII with the resulting crystallographic (.cif) structure available and visualized in Fig S12b. The final unit cell is then thermally relaxed by rigid-body NPT at 300K, with independent barostats on each axis such that the force fields set the lattice and herringbone arrangements. Over this range the minimum enthalpy cell produces tilt of 72(1) and density of 1.657 g/cm3 against 72.9(4) and 1.64(3) g/cm3 from RSoXS and reproduces the lamellar and (002) spacings within 1.5%. The final relaxed unit cell is visualized in Fig S12c used in the remaining MD simulations. Real space molecular visualization: Molecular packing in Fig. 4c is molecular dynamics (MD) reconstruction of the film. It is built from the fitted depth profiles of Fig 4a,b and relaxed in LAMMPS.69 ZnPc is treated as rigid body in the molecular frame used for the DFT calculations. Lennard-Jones parameters are taken from GAFF2, with UFF for Zn, and atomic charges are fitted to the B3LYP/def2-SVP electrostatic potential. This force field reproduces the 𝛽-ZnPc unit cell at 100K to within 1.5% on each axis (SI). The film is constructed for pure visualization by data fusion with the fitted depth profiles, GIXRD, and the fitted electrostatic potentials. The molecular frame is the same used for the DFT calculations (C32H16N8Zn, 𝑀 = 577.9 g/mol). Its van der Waals envelope gives an in-plane diameter of 14.5 Å and faceto-face thickness of 3.6 Å, and the 𝜋-stacking separation is taken as 3.4 Å. At each depth 𝑧 the molecular tilt is 𝛾(𝑧) from the orientation profile, and the area per molecule in the drawing plane is 𝑀/(𝜌(𝑧)𝑁𝐴𝑡), with 𝜌(𝑧) the fitted density profile and 𝑡 = 14.4 Å the extrusion thickness of the slab that the projection represents. The packing density of the molecules in the illustration is therefore self-consistent with the density and orientation gradients from Fig 4b&d. The projected cell is orthogonal, carrying lamellar period along 𝑧 and column period in plane whose ratio is fixed by the molecular diameter, the 𝜋 stacking separation and sin2(𝛾(𝑧)). The lamellae period is modified by the interdigitation between neighboring lamellae, set by dimensionless factor 𝑓 = 0.96, so adjacent layers can overlap by 4% of the molecular diameter. This together with the herringbone splay and positional and orientational disorder are set only for visual continuity and are neither empirical nor derived factors. The depth dependent lamellae and 𝜋 d-spacings are compared with diffraction orders derived from experimental GIWAXS measurements in Fig S11. Because both the cell area and its aspect ratio vary with depth, each monolayer contributed its own pair of spacings rather than single value, so the predicted diffraction positions are taken as the maxima of these depth distributions, weighted by the local density and the DebyeWaller factor built from the drawn positional disorder.
